overview: This bill would require the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Federal Reserve to jointly study two tools for selling failed banks. A "shelf charter" is a conditional approval for an investor group without a bank to quickly get a charter so it can buy a failing bank, and the FDIC's "modified bidder qualification process" lets such groups bid on failed banks. The study would look at how these tools have been used since 2008, whether wider use during the 2023 bank failures could have drawn more buyers, protected the deposit insurance fund or avoided emergency measures, and the benefits and risks of private equity firms owning banks this way. A report with recommendations would be due to Congress within one year. As of February 25, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was awaiting a vote by the full House.
for: Supporters say more potential buyers for failing banks could mean better prices, less cost to the deposit insurance fund and less reliance on emergency rescues or mergers that make big banks bigger.
against: Critics say the study could pave the way for more private equity ownership of banks, which some view as riskier because such owners may seek quick returns rather than long-term stability.
